hints.medium: Subtract the number of protons from the mass number to find the neutrons.

questions.text: What is the general purpose of a universal indicator?

options.text: To show a range of colors corresponding to different pH levels
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike single-color indicators, a universal indicator shows a whole spectrum of colors across the pH scale.

options.text: To measure the temperature of a solution
options.feedback: A universal indicator measures pH (acidity/basicity), not temperature.

options.text: To measure the exact mass of a solution
options.feedback: Mass measurement isn't the purpose of a pH indicator -- it's specifically about showing acidity/basicity via color.

options.text: To make a solution taste different
options.feedback: Indicators are visual tools showing color change, not something that affects taste.

hints.hard: This tool visually reveals a solution's approximate position along the full acid-to-base spectrum.
hints.medium: This tool shows a whole range of colors depending on how acidic or basic something is.
hints.easy: This tool changes into different colors depending on how acidic or basic something is.

questions.text: A universal indicator turns red in one solution and dark blue/purple in another. What does this suggest about the two solutions?

options.text: The red solution is strongly acidic, while the dark blue/purple solution is strongly basic
options.feedback: Correct -- universal indicators typically show red for strong acids and blue/purple for strong bases, with green representing neutral.

options.text: Both solutions have exactly the same pH
options.feedback: Different colors specifically indicate DIFFERENT pH levels -- if they had the same pH, the indicator would show the same color for both.

options.text: The red solution is basic, and the blue solution is acidic
options.feedback: This is backwards for a standard universal indicator -- red typically signals acidic, and blue/purple typically signals basic.

options.text: This color difference has nothing to do with pH
options.feedback: This color difference is specifically and directly tied to the pH difference between the two solutions.

hints.hard: Recall the typical color-coding convention: warm colors (red/orange) for acidic, cool colors (blue/purple) for basic, with green in the middle for neutral.
hints.medium: Remember that red typically signals strong acid, and blue/purple typically signals strong base on this type of indicator.
hints.easy: Red usually means acidic, and blue/purple usually means basic.

questions.text: Different indicators (like litmus, phenolphthalein, and universal indicator) change color at different, specific pH ranges. Why might a chemist choose a specific indicator rather than always using a universal indicator?

options.text: A specific indicator with a narrow, well-defined color-change range can more precisely pinpoint whether a solution has crossed a particular pH threshold relevant to their experiment
options.feedback: Correct -- for identifying a precise endpoint (like in a titration), a sharp, specific color change at a known pH is often more useful than a broad, gradual color spectrum.

options.text: There is no real reason -- all indicators work identically in every situation
options.feedback: Different indicators actually have genuinely different, useful properties (specific color-change pH ranges) suited to different experimental needs.

options.text: Specific indicators are always cheaper than universal indicators, which is the only reason for choosing them
options.feedback: While cost might be A factor, the PRIMARY scientific reason for choosing a specific indicator relates to its precise, well-defined pH transition range, not simply cost.

options.text: Specific indicators can only be used with acids, never with bases
options.feedback: Specific indicators can be selected for use across various points along the pH scale, working with both acid-related and base-related transitions depending on the indicator chosen.

hints.hard: A narrow-range indicator provides a sharp, unambiguous color change precisely at a known pH value, which is more useful for detecting a specific threshold than a gradual, broad-spectrum color shift.
hints.medium: A specific indicator gives a sharp, clear color change right at one particular pH point, which is more useful for pinpointing an exact moment in an experiment.
hints.easy: A specific indicator gives one clear, sudden color change right at a useful pH point, unlike the gradual rainbow of a universal indicator.

questions.text: In a chemical reaction, what determines the elements that can appear in the products?

options.text: The elements that were present in the reactants -- no new elements can be created in a normal chemical reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- chemical reactions only rearrange existing atoms into new combinations; they don't create or destroy elements.

options.text: Any element the chemist wants can simply appear in the products
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- ordinary chemical reactions can't introduce entirely new elements not already present in the reactants.

options.text: Products always contain completely different elements from the reactants
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- products are made of the SAME elements originally present in the reactants, just rearranged into new combinations.

options.text: Only reactions involving oxygen can determine product elements
options.feedback: This applies to all chemical reactions generally, not something unique to reactions specifically involving oxygen.

hints.hard: Chemical reactions rearrange existing atomic building blocks rather than creating entirely new ones.
hints.medium: A chemical reaction can only rearrange atoms that were already there to begin with.
hints.easy: A chemical reaction can only rearrange the atoms that were already there.

questions.text: If a reaction starts with only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, why is it impossible for one of the products to contain nitrogen?

options.text: Chemical reactions cannot create new elements -- nitrogen atoms would have to already be present in the reactants for them to appear in a product
options.feedback: Correct -- this reflects the fundamental principle of conservation of elements/mass in chemical reactions.

options.text: Nitrogen atoms can spontaneously appear during any chemical reaction
options.feedback: This isn't possible under normal chemical reactions -- elements are conserved, not created, during typical chemistry.

options.text: This is actually possible and happens routinely in chemical reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot create entirely new elements not present among the original reactants.

options.text: Nitrogen is a special element that follows completely different rules
options.feedback: Nitrogen follows the same fundamental principle as every other element -- reactions can't create elements not already present in the reactants.

hints.hard: Consider the fundamental principle that chemical processes conserve the identity and quantity of every element present throughout the reaction.
hints.medium: Since nitrogen wasn't part of the starting materials, there's no way for it to just show up in the products.
hints.easy: Since nitrogen wasn't in the starting materials, it can't just show up in the products.

questions.text: Nuclear reactions, unlike ordinary chemical reactions, CAN actually transform one element into a different element entirely. Why does this fundamental distinction exist between chemical and nuclear processes?

options.text: Chemical reactions only involve rearranging electrons and bonds between atoms, while nuclear reactions involve changes within the atomic nucleus itself (protons/neutrons), which is what actually determines an element's identity
options.feedback: Correct -- since an element's identity is defined by its number of protons, only a nuclear-level change (unlike ordinary electron-based chemical bonding) can transform one element into another.

options.text: There is actually no real distinction between chemical and nuclear reactions
options.feedback: There is a very real, fundamental distinction -- chemical reactions involve electron rearrangement, while nuclear reactions involve changes to the nucleus itself, which is why only nuclear reactions can transmute elements.

options.text: Chemical reactions actually can transform elements just as easily as nuclear reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot change one element into another; that specifically requires a nuclear-level process.

options.text: Nuclear reactions don't actually involve atoms at all
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions definitely involve atoms -- specifically, changes occurring within their nuclei, which is the key distinguishing feature from ordinary chemical reactions.

hints.hard: An element's identity is defined specifically by its proton count, which chemical (electron-level) reactions cannot alter -- only nuclear-level processes affecting the proton count can transmute one element into another.
hints.medium: Chemical reactions only mess with the outer electrons, but changing what element something IS requires actually changing its nucleus, which only nuclear reactions can do.
hints.easy: Chemical reactions only mess with outer electrons, but changing what element something is requires changing its nucleus.

questions.text: If two samples both have the exact chemical formula H₂O and are pure, will they have the same physical properties (like boiling point)?

options.text: Yes, since they are chemically identical, their fundamental properties will be the same under the same conditions
options.feedback: Correct -- pure samples of the same compound share identical chemical and physical properties under matching conditions.

options.text: No, they will always have completely different properties
options.feedback: Pure samples of the exact same compound should have identical properties under the same conditions, not different ones.

options.text: It depends entirely on which country the water came from
options.feedback: Geographic origin doesn't affect the fundamental properties of a pure chemical compound -- its formula and structure do.

options.text: Properties are always completely random for any substance
options.feedback: Chemical and physical properties are actually determined by a substance's specific composition and structure, not randomness.

hints.hard: Chemically identical substances should exhibit identical characteristic behaviors under matching physical conditions.
hints.medium: Since they're the exact same pure substance, they should behave exactly the same way.
hints.easy: Since it's the exact same pure substance, it should act the same way every time.

questions.text: Why can chemists reliably predict a pure compound's properties (like melting point) just from knowing its identity, without needing to test every single sample?

options.text: A pure compound's properties are consistently determined by its fixed chemical composition and structure, which don't vary between different pure samples of the same substance
options.feedback: Correct -- this reliability and reproducibility of properties is a foundational principle that makes chemistry a predictive science.

options.text: Chemists actually cannot predict any compound's properties in advance
options.feedback: This isn't true -- chemists rely heavily on established properties of known pure compounds precisely because these properties are consistent and predictable.

options.text: Every single sample of a pure compound has completely different, unpredictable properties
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- properties of a pure compound are consistent and reproducible, not unpredictably variable between samples.

options.text: This predictability has nothing to do with chemical composition
options.feedback: This predictability is actually directly rooted in a compound's fixed, well-defined chemical composition and structure.

hints.hard: This predictability stems from the direct causal link between a compound's fixed molecular structure/bonding and its resulting physical/chemical behavior.
hints.medium: A pure compound's structure directly determines its properties, and that structure doesn't change from sample to sample.
hints.easy: A pure compound's structure stays the same, so its properties stay the same too.

questions.text: If a sample labeled as 'pure water' shows a boiling point significantly different from 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure, what would this most likely indicate?

options.text: The sample is likely not actually pure -- it probably contains dissolved impurities that are altering its boiling point
options.feedback: Correct -- deviations from a substance's known, expected properties are often used as practical evidence that a sample isn't as pure as claimed.

options.text: Water's boiling point actually varies randomly with no explanation
options.feedback: Water's boiling point at a given standard pressure is a well-established, consistent value -- an unexpected result more likely points to impurities or non-standard conditions.

options.text: The measurement definitely proves nothing unusual is happening
options.feedback: A significant deviation from the expected value for a supposedly pure substance IS a meaningful, notable finding worth investigating (likely impurities).

options.text: This result has no scientific significance at all
options.feedback: This kind of unexpected result actually has real scientific significance -- it's a practical, useful signal suggesting the sample may not be genuinely pure.

hints.hard: Established reference properties (like boiling point at standard pressure) serve as a diagnostic benchmark -- significant deviation strongly suggests the presence of contaminants altering the substance's expected behavior.
hints.medium: If something dissolved is mixed in with the water, it can change the boiling point away from the normal expected value.
hints.easy: If something else is mixed in with the water, it can change the boiling point away from normal.

hints.easy: Divide 6 by 2.

questions.text: Using the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, if 10 moles of H₂ react with 3 moles of O₂, which reactant is the limiting reactant, and how much water (in moles) is produced?

options.text: Oxygen is limiting; 6 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: Correct -- 3 moles of O₂ would need 6 moles of H₂ (2:1 ratio), but 10 are available, so oxygen runs out first, and 3 moles O₂ produces 2×3=6 moles of H₂O.

options.text: Hydrogen is limiting; 10 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: There's actually more than enough hydrogen available relative to the oxygen present -- oxygen is the one that runs out first.

options.text: Oxygen is limiting; 3 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: While oxygen is correctly identified as limiting, the water produced should be DOUBLE the oxygen amount (2:2 ratio in the equation), giving 6, not 3.

options.text: Neither reactant is limiting; both are used up completely
options.feedback: One reactant must run out first in this scenario -- checking the required ratio shows oxygen is the limiting reactant, with hydrogen left over.

questions.text: Compared to pure water, does salt water generally boil at a higher or lower temperature?

options.text: Higher
options.feedback: Correct -- dissolved salt raises the boiling point above that of pure water, a phenomenon called boiling point elevation.

options.text: Lower
options.feedback: This is backwards -- dissolved salt actually raises the boiling point, not lowers it.

options.text: Exactly the same temperature
options.feedback: Dissolved salt does have a measurable effect, raising the boiling point above that of pure water.

options.text: Salt water doesn't boil at all
options.feedback: Salt water absolutely can and does boil -- just at a slightly higher temperature than pure water.

hints.hard: Consider whether dissolving something in a liquid typically raises or lowers the temperature needed for it to boil.
hints.medium: Think about whether adding something dissolved usually makes it easier or harder for the liquid to boil.
hints.easy: Adding salt makes it a little harder for the water to boil, needing more heat.

questions.text: Why does adding salt to water raise its boiling point?

options.text: The dissolved salt particles interfere with water molecules escaping into vapor, requiring more energy (higher temperature) to reach boiling
options.feedback: Correct -- dissolved particles disrupt the process of water molecules leaving the liquid phase, requiring additional thermal energy to compensate.

options.text: Salt directly makes the water molecules move faster
options.feedback: The effect isn't about directly speeding up water molecules -- it's about the dissolved particles interfering with the vaporization process itself.

options.text: Salt has no actual effect on water's boiling point
options.feedback: Salt does have a measurable, real effect on boiling point, specifically raising it -- this is well-documented chemistry (boiling point elevation).

options.text: Salt actually cools the water down, which is why it takes longer to boil
options.feedback: The higher boiling point isn't due to net cooling -- it's due to the dissolved particles' interference with the phase-change (vaporization) process itself.

hints.hard: Dissolved particles occupy space at the liquid's surface, physically hindering the escape of solvent molecules into the vapor phase.
hints.medium: The dissolved salt particles get in the way of water molecules trying to escape into steam.
hints.easy: The dissolved salt particles get in the way of water molecules trying to turn into steam.

questions.text: Boiling point elevation depends on the NUMBER of dissolved particles, not necessarily their specific chemical identity. Why would adding the same molar amount of sugar versus salt to water have different effects on boiling point elevation?

options.text: Salt (like NaCl) dissociates into two separate ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) in water, effectively doubling the number of dissolved particles compared to the same molar amount of sugar, which doesn't dissociate at all
options.feedback: Correct -- since boiling point elevation depends on total particle count, salt's dissociation into two ions produces roughly double the effect of a non-dissociating solute like sugar at the same molarity.

options.text: Sugar and salt would have the exact same effect on boiling point, since they're added in the same molar amount
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- salt's ionic dissociation into two separate particles per formula unit gives it roughly double the boiling-point-elevating effect compared to sugar at the same molarity.

options.text: Sugar always has a stronger effect on boiling point than salt
options.feedback: This is backwards -- salt's dissociation into multiple ions typically gives it a STRONGER effect per mole than a non-dissociating solute like sugar.

options.text: This effect has nothing to do with the number of dissolved particles
options.feedback: This effect is actually directly and fundamentally tied to the total number of dissolved particles in solution, which is precisely why dissociation matters.

hints.hard: Boiling point elevation is a colligative property dependent on total solute particle concentration -- ionic compounds that dissociate into multiple ions per formula unit produce a proportionally larger effect than non-dissociating molecular solutes at equal molarity.
hints.medium: Salt splits apart into two separate charged pieces once dissolved, so it actually creates twice as many dissolved "things" as the same amount of sugar, which stays as one piece.
hints.easy: Salt splits into two separate pieces in water, so it creates twice as many dissolved bits as the same amount of sugar.

questions.text: Rusting of iron is an example of what type of chemical reaction?

options.text: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- rusting involves iron losing electrons (oxidizing) while oxygen gains them (reducing).

options.text: A neutralization reaction

options.text: A nuclear reaction
options.feedback: Rusting is an ordinary chemical process, not a nuclear reaction, which would involve changes to atomic nuclei.

options.text: No reaction occurs during rusting
options.feedback: Rusting is very much a real, observable chemical reaction between iron and oxygen (often with water present).

hints.hard: This reaction category is defined by simultaneous electron loss and electron gain between two participating substances.
hints.medium: This is the same broad category of reaction as electron transfer between substances.
hints.easy: This reaction involves iron and oxygen swapping electrons.

questions.text: Why does rusting typically happen faster in humid or wet environments compared to very dry ones?

options.text: Water acts as a medium that facilitates the electron transfer (redox) process between iron and oxygen, speeding up the reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- water helps ions move and interact more effectively, accelerating the overall rusting reaction.

options.text: Water actually prevents rusting from happening at all
options.feedback: This is backwards -- water generally SPEEDS UP rusting, rather than preventing it, by facilitating the necessary electron transfer process.

options.text: Humidity has no actual effect on the rusting process
options.feedback: Humidity does have a significant, well-documented effect on rusting rate, generally accelerating it.

options.text: Rusting only happens underwater, never in humid air
options.feedback: Rusting can happen in humid air (not just fully submerged underwater) -- moisture in the air is enough to facilitate and speed up the reaction.

hints.hard: Ionic movement and interaction, which drive electron transfer, are facilitated by the presence of a liquid medium like water.

hints.easy: Water helps speed up the electron-swapping process that causes rust.

questions.text: Galvanized steel (steel coated with a layer of zinc) resists rusting even if the zinc coating gets scratched, exposing the steel underneath. Why does this protection persist even after the coating is damaged?

options.text: Zinc is more easily oxidized than iron, so the zinc will preferentially corrode (sacrificially) instead of the exposed iron, as long as some zinc remains in contact
options.feedback: Correct -- this 'sacrificial protection' strategy relies on zinc's greater tendency to oxidize, protecting the iron underneath even with some coating damage.

options.text: The scratch actually makes the zinc coating irrelevant, and rusting proceeds unaffected regardless
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- the remaining zinc coating continues to provide meaningful sacrificial protection even after a scratch, as long as it's still in electrical contact with the exposed steel.

options.text: Zinc is less reactive than iron, which is why it protects the steel
options.feedback: This is backwards -- zinc is actually MORE reactive (more easily oxidized) than iron, and this greater reactivity is exactly why it sacrificially protects the steel.

options.text: This protective effect has nothing to do with the relative reactivity of the two metals
options.feedback: This protective effect is actually directly and specifically explained by the relative reactivity difference between zinc and iron.

hints.hard: A more reactive metal (zinc) will preferentially undergo oxidation ahead of a less reactive one (iron) when both are exposed and electrically connected, providing ongoing protection to the iron as long as sacrificial zinc remains available.

hints.easy: Since zinc reacts more easily than iron, it corrodes first instead, protecting the iron underneath.

questions.text: What is electron shielding?

options.text: A physical shield made of metal placed around an atom
options.feedback: This isn't a literal physical object -- it's an electronic effect involving how electrons interact with the nucleus's pull.

options.text: The process of an atom losing all its electrons
options.feedback: Electron shielding is about the interaction between existing electrons and the nucleus, not about losing electrons entirely.

options.text: A technique for protecting atoms from radioactivity
options.feedback: This isn't related to radiation protection -- it's specifically about how inner electrons affect the nuclear attraction felt by outer electrons.

hints.hard: This effect describes how electrons closer to the nucleus can partially block the nuclear pull experienced by more distant electrons.
hints.medium: This describes how inner electrons can partly block the nucleus's pull on outer electrons.
hints.easy: This is how inner electrons partly block the nucleus's pull on the outer ones.

questions.text: Why does atomic radius generally increase as you move down a group (column) on the periodic table?

options.text: Each additional electron shell increases both the distance from the nucleus and the shielding effect, both of which contribute to a larger atomic size

questions.text: Carbon dioxide (CO2) has polar C=O bonds, yet the overall molecule is nonpolar. How can a molecule with polar bonds still be a nonpolar molecule overall?

options.text: Because CO2's linear, symmetric shape causes the two equal but opposite bond dipoles to cancel each other out, resulting in no net molecular dipole
options.feedback: Correct -- molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity AND molecular geometry; symmetric arrangements can cause individual bond dipoles to cancel out.

options.text: The C=O bonds in CO2 are not actually polar at all
options.feedback: The C=O bonds ARE genuinely polar due to the electronegativity difference between carbon and oxygen -- the molecule's overall nonpolarity comes from its symmetric shape, not from nonpolar bonds.

options.text: Molecular polarity depends only on bond polarity and never on molecular shape
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- molecular shape plays a critical role alongside bond polarity in determining overall molecular polarity, as seen in CO2's case.

options.text: CO2 is actually a polar molecule, not nonpolar
options.feedback: CO2 is a well-established example of a nonpolar molecule, despite containing individually polar bonds, due to its symmetric linear geometry.

hints.hard: Consider how the vector sum of individual bond dipole moments is affected by the molecule's overall symmetric geometry.
hints.medium: Think about how the molecule's straight, symmetric shape might cause the two pulling directions to cancel each other out.
hints.easy: The molecule's straight, symmetric shape lets the two pulls cancel each other out.

questions.text: How does a catalyst manage to speed up a reaction without being consumed?

options.text: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, then is released unchanged after facilitating the reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- by lowering the energy barrier reactants must overcome, a catalyst allows more successful collisions per unit time, all while being regenerated afterward.

options.text: It increases the activation energy needed, forcing the reaction to happen faster
options.feedback: This is backwards -- a catalyst LOWERS the activation energy required, not increases it, which is what allows the reaction to proceed faster.

options.text: It adds extra energy directly into the reactant molecules permanently
options.feedback: A catalyst doesn't permanently add energy to reactants -- it provides a lower-energy pathway for the reaction to proceed, without being altered itself.

options.text: Catalysts have no actual mechanism -- they just randomly speed up reactions
options.feedback: There is a well-understood mechanism: catalysts lower the activation energy barrier by providing an alternative reaction pathway.

hints.hard: Consider how offering a lower-energy route for reactants to follow increases the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy to react.
hints.medium: By giving the reaction an easier path with a lower energy requirement, more collisions succeed in a given time.
hints.easy: By lowering the energy needed to react, more molecules can successfully react in a given time.

questions.text: A catalyst increases reaction rate by lowering activation energy, but it does NOT change the overall energy difference between reactants and products (the reaction's enthalpy change). Why is this distinction important?

options.text: Because it shows a catalyst only affects HOW FAST equilibrium is reached, not WHERE that equilibrium lies or how much net energy is released/absorbed overall
options.feedback: Correct -- this distinction (kinetics vs. thermodynamics) is fundamental: catalysts affect reaction rate/kinetics, not the fundamental energetics or equilibrium position of the reaction.

options.text: It isn't actually an important distinction -- catalysts change both the rate and the overall energy released
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- catalysts specifically do NOT change the overall enthalpy change of a reaction, only its rate, which IS an important distinction in chemistry.

options.text: Because catalysts actually do change the final equilibrium position of a reaction
options.feedback: Catalysts do NOT shift a reaction's equilibrium position -- they only affect how quickly that (unchanged) equilibrium is reached.

options.text: Because activation energy and enthalpy change are actually the exact same quantity
options.feedback: These are distinct concepts -- activation energy is the barrier height to overcome, while enthalpy change is the net energy difference between reactants and products.

hints.hard: Separate the concept of reaction speed (kinetics, governed by activation energy) from the concept of net energy change (thermodynamics, governed by enthalpy) -- a catalyst only affects the former.
hints.medium: A catalyst changes how quickly a reaction happens, but not how much total energy the reaction releases or absorbs overall.
hints.easy: A catalyst changes how fast a reaction happens, but not how much energy it releases overall.

questions.text: What does Le Chatelier's principle describe?

options.text: How a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract a change imposed on it
options.feedback: Correct -- the system responds by shifting the reaction to partially offset whatever disturbance was introduced.

options.text: How to calculate the exact rate of a chemical reaction
options.feedback: Reaction rate calculations are a different topic -- Le Chatelier's principle is about how equilibrium position responds to disturbances.

options.text: How atoms bond together to form molecules
options.feedback: Bonding theory is a separate topic from Le Chatelier's principle, which concerns equilibrium shifts.

options.text: How to determine the mass of a compound
options.feedback: Mass calculations (stoichiometry) are unrelated to Le Chatelier's principle.

hints.hard: This principle addresses how a system in dynamic balance responds to counteract externally imposed disturbances.
hints.medium: This describes how a balanced reaction shifts to fight back against a change made to it.
hints.easy: This describes how a balanced reaction shifts to fight back against a change.

questions.text: For the reaction N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, if more N2 gas is added to the system at equilibrium, which direction will the equilibrium shift?

options.text: Forward (toward NH3), to partially consume the added N2 and reduce the disturbance
options.feedback: Correct -- adding a reactant shifts equilibrium toward the products, consuming some of the added substance to counteract the change.

options.text: Backward (toward N2 and H2), moving further away from equilibrium
options.feedback: This is backwards -- adding a reactant shifts equilibrium FORWARD (toward products), not backward, in an attempt to counteract the added substance.

options.text: The equilibrium won't shift at all, since adding reactant has no effect
options.feedback: Adding a reactant does have a real effect according to Le Chatelier's principle -- it shifts the equilibrium forward toward products.

options.text: The reaction will completely stop occurring
options.feedback: The reaction doesn't stop -- it continues, just with a shift in the equilibrium position toward producing more product.

hints.hard: Consider which direction would partially consume the newly added substance, restoring some balance to the system.
hints.medium: Adding more of a starting ingredient pushes the reaction to make more of the other side, using up some of what was added.
hints.easy: Adding more N2 pushes the reaction to make more NH3, using up some of the extra N2.

questions.text: For the same reaction (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, which is exothermic in the forward direction), why would increasing the temperature actually shift the equilibrium AWAY from NH3 production, even though heating usually speeds up reactions?

options.text: Because the system treats added heat like an extra 'product' of an exothermic reaction, so it shifts backward (favoring the endothermic reverse reaction) to absorb the excess heat
options.feedback: Correct -- for exothermic reactions, increasing temperature shifts equilibrium toward the reactants (favoring the heat-absorbing reverse direction), even though the raw reaction RATE for both directions increases.

options.text: Temperature actually has no effect on chemical equilibrium position, only on reaction rate
options.feedback: Temperature very much affects equilibrium POSITION for reactions involving heat (exothermic/endothermic), not just reaction rate.

options.text: Since heating always speeds up a reaction, it must always shift equilibrium toward the products, regardless of the reaction's heat effects
options.feedback: This conflates reaction rate with equilibrium position -- for an EXOTHERMIC reaction specifically, increased temperature actually shifts equilibrium toward reactants, not products.

options.text: This reaction doesn't actually reach any equilibrium state at any temperature
options.feedback: This reaction, like many reversible reactions, does reach an equilibrium state -- temperature changes shift WHERE that equilibrium lies, not whether it's reached.

hints.hard: Treat heat as if it were a reactant or product depending on the reaction's thermal nature, then apply the same disturbance-counteracting logic used for concentration changes.
hints.medium: Since this reaction releases heat going forward, adding more heat pushes the reaction backward, to use up that extra heat.
hints.easy: Since this reaction releases heat going forward, adding more heat pushes the reaction backward instead.

questions.text: What is a 'limiting reactant' in a chemical reaction?

options.text: The reactant that is completely used up first, stopping the reaction and limiting how much product can form
options.feedback: Correct -- once the limiting reactant runs out, the reaction cannot proceed further, regardless of how much of the other reactant remains.

options.text: The reactant that is left over in excess after the reaction
options.feedback: That describes the 'excess reactant' -- the limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, not the one left over.

options.text: The reactant with the largest molar mass
options.feedback: Molar mass alone doesn't determine which reactant is limiting -- it depends on the amounts present relative to the reaction's stoichiometry.

options.text: The reactant that reacts the slowest
options.feedback: Reaction speed (kinetics) is a separate concept from which reactant is limiting, which is about quantity relative to stoichiometric need.

hints.hard: This is the reactant whose depletion halts further product formation, regardless of remaining quantities of other reactants.
hints.medium: This is the ingredient that runs out first, stopping the reaction from making any more product.
hints.easy: This is the ingredient that runs out first, stopping the reaction.

questions.text: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, you have 4 moles of H2 and 1 mole of O2. Which is the limiting reactant?

options.text: O2, since only 1 mole of O2 is needed to fully react with the 4 moles of H2 (2 moles of H2 react per mole of O2), leaving no O2 left over
options.feedback: Correct -- 4 moles H2 requires exactly 2 moles O2 to react completely, but only 1 mole O2 is available, and O2 runs out first, leaving excess H2 unreacted.

options.text: H2, since there is more of it than O2
options.feedback: Having a larger quantity doesn't automatically make a reactant limiting -- it depends on the required stoichiometric ratio, not just raw amount.

options.text: Neither is limiting, since both reactants will be completely used up
options.feedback: Checking the stoichiometric ratio shows one reactant DOES run out first (O2), leaving excess H2 -- they aren't both fully consumed.

options.text: This reaction doesn't have a limiting reactant
options.feedback: Nearly all reactions with a specific given ratio of reactants have a limiting reactant, unless the reactants happen to be provided in the exact stoichiometric ratio.

hints.hard: Compare the available mole ratio of the reactants to the required stoichiometric ratio from the balanced equation to identify which runs out first.
hints.medium: Check how much O2 is actually needed for all the H2 to react, then compare to how much O2 you actually have.
hints.easy: You need 2 moles of O2 for 4 moles of H2, but you only have 1 mole of O2 -- so O2 runs out first.

questions.text: Using the same reaction and initial amounts (4 moles H2, 1 mole O2, with O2 as the limiting reactant), how many moles of water (H2O) will actually be produced?

options.text: 2 moles, since 1 mole of O2 produces 2 moles of H2O according to the balanced equation's 2:1 ratio of products to O2
options.feedback: Correct -- since O2 is limiting and the equation shows 1 mole O2 yields 2 moles H2O, all 1 mole of available O2 produces exactly 2 moles of H2O.

options.text: 4 moles, based on the amount of H2 available
options.feedback: Since O2 is the LIMITING reactant, product yield must be calculated based on O2's available quantity, not H2's (since not all H2 will actually get to react).

options.text: 1 mole, matching the amount of O2 present
options.feedback: This doesn't correctly apply the reaction's stoichiometric ratio -- 1 mole of O2 actually yields 2 moles of H2O, not 1 mole.

options.text: 5 moles, adding together the reactant amounts
options.feedback: Simply adding reactant amounts doesn't reflect how stoichiometry determines product yield -- yield must be calculated from the limiting reactant's amount and the balanced equation's ratios.

hints.hard: Use the limiting reactant's molar amount together with the balanced equation's mole ratio between that reactant and the product to calculate maximum yield.
hints.medium: Since O2 is limiting, use its amount and the equation's ratio (1 mole O2 makes 2 moles H2O) to find the product amount.
hints.easy: Since O2 is limiting, and 1 mole O2 makes 2 moles of water, the answer is 2 moles.

questions.text: On the pH scale (0-14), what does a pH value below 7 indicate?

options.text: The solution is acidic
options.feedback: Correct -- pH values below 7 indicate acidity, with lower values being more strongly acidic.

options.text: The solution is basic (alkaline)
options.feedback: Basic solutions have a pH ABOVE 7, not below it.

options.text: The solution is perfectly neutral
options.feedback: Neutral solutions have a pH of exactly 7, not below it.

options.text: The solution contains no water
options.feedback: pH doesn't indicate water content -- it measures the concentration of hydrogen ions, which relates to acidity/basicity.

hints.hard: Values below the scale's midpoint on this measure correspond to a higher concentration of hydrogen ions.
hints.medium: Lower numbers on this scale mean the solution has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions.
hints.easy: Lower numbers on this scale mean more acidic.

questions.text: The pH scale is logarithmic, meaning each whole number change represents a 10-fold change in hydrogen ion concentration. How many times more acidic is a solution with pH 3 compared to one with pH 5?

options.text: 100 times more acidic (10² since the difference is 2 pH units)
options.feedback: Correct -- since each pH unit represents a 10-fold change, a 2-unit difference means 10×10 = 100 times more hydrogen ion concentration.

options.text: 2 times more acidic
options.feedback: This treats the pH scale as linear, but it's actually logarithmic -- a difference of 2 pH units means a 100-fold difference, not just 2 times.

options.text: 20 times more acidic
options.feedback: This doesn't correctly apply the logarithmic (powers of 10) relationship between pH units.

options.text: 10 times more acidic
options.feedback: 10 times would be correct for just a ONE-unit pH difference, but here the difference is 2 units, requiring 10×10=100.

hints.hard: Since each single unit represents a factor-of-10 change, calculate 10 raised to the power of the total pH unit difference.
hints.medium: Since each pH unit is a factor of 10, and the difference here is 2 units, multiply 10 by itself.
hints.easy: Since the difference is 2 pH units, multiply 10 times 10 to get 100.

questions.text: A strong acid and a weak acid can have the same molar concentration but different pH values. Why does a strong acid typically have a lower pH (more acidic) than a weak acid at the same concentration?

options.text: A strong acid fully dissociates into ions in solution, releasing the maximum possible hydrogen ions, while a weak acid only partially dissociates, releasing fewer free hydrogen ions
options.feedback: Correct -- this difference in dissociation degree (not just initial concentration) is exactly what determines the actual free hydrogen ion concentration, and thus the resulting pH.

options.text: Strong acids and weak acids always have identical pH values at the same concentration
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- differing degrees of dissociation between strong and weak acids lead to genuinely different pH values, even at equal starting concentrations.

options.text: Weak acids actually release MORE hydrogen ions than strong acids at the same concentration
options.feedback: This is backwards -- strong acids fully dissociate and release MORE free hydrogen ions than weak acids (which only partially dissociate) at the same starting concentration.

options.text: The strength of an acid has nothing to do with how much it dissociates in solution
options.feedback: Acid strength is DEFINED by degree of dissociation -- strong acids dissociate completely, while weak acids only dissociate partially, which is the key distinguishing factor here.

hints.hard: Distinguish between a substance's overall (analytical) concentration and the actual concentration of free ions it releases upon dissociation in solution.
hints.medium: A strong acid breaks apart completely in water, releasing all its hydrogen ions, while a weak acid only breaks apart partway.
hints.easy: A strong acid breaks apart completely, releasing all its hydrogen ions, while a weak acid only breaks apart partway.

questions.text: In a redox reaction, what happens during 'oxidation'?

options.text: A substance loses electrons
options.feedback: Correct -- oxidation specifically refers to the loss of electrons by a substance (remember: OIL = Oxidation Is Loss).

options.text: A substance gains electrons
options.feedback: That describes reduction, the opposite of oxidation (remember: RIG = Reduction Is Gain).

options.text: A substance gains protons
options.feedback: Redox reactions concern electron transfer, not proton transfer -- proton transfer is central to acid-base reactions instead.

options.text: A substance's mass increases significantly
options.feedback: Oxidation is defined by electron loss, not by any significant mass change of the substance.

hints.hard: This half-reaction involves a substance relinquishing negatively charged electron particles.
hints.medium: This is when a substance loses electrons during a reaction.
hints.easy: This is when a substance loses electrons.

questions.text: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc metal loses two electrons to become Zn²⁺, while Cu²⁺ gains two electrons to become copper metal. Which substance is oxidized, and which is reduced?

options.text: Zinc is oxidized (loses electrons); Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains electrons)
options.feedback: Correct -- zinc loses electrons (oxidation) while copper ions gain those electrons (reduction), making this a classic redox reaction.

options.text: Zinc is reduced; Cu²⁺ is oxidized
options.feedback: This has the roles reversed -- zinc LOSES electrons (oxidation), while Cu²⁺ GAINS electrons (reduction), not the other way around.

options.text: Both substances are oxidized simultaneously
options.feedback: In any redox reaction, oxidation and reduction always occur together as a pair -- one substance can't be oxidized without another being reduced.

options.text: Neither substance undergoes any electron transfer in this reaction
options.feedback: This reaction is a textbook example specifically involving electron transfer -- zinc loses electrons while copper ions gain them.

hints.hard: Track the direction of electron movement for each substance individually to determine which one is losing versus gaining electrons.
hints.medium: Zinc goes from neutral to Zn²⁺ (losing electrons), while copper ions go from Cu²⁺ to neutral copper (gaining electrons).
hints.easy: Zinc loses electrons to become Zn²⁺, so zinc is oxidized. Copper gains those electrons, so it's reduced.

questions.text: In this same reaction (Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu), zinc is called the 'reducing agent.' Why is the substance that gets oxidized called the reducing agent, rather than the 'oxidizing agent'?

options.text: Because zinc's own oxidation (losing electrons) is what CAUSES the reduction of the other substance (Cu²⁺), so it acts as the agent enabling that reduction
options.feedback: Correct -- naming conventions in redox reactions are based on what a substance CAUSES to happen to the other reactant, not what happens to itself, which is why the oxidized substance is termed the reducing agent.

options.text: This naming convention is simply an arbitrary error in chemistry terminology
options.feedback: This is not an error -- it's a deliberate, standard convention based on what effect each substance has on the OTHER reactant, not on itself.

options.text: Zinc is actually the one being reduced in this reaction, not oxidized
options.feedback: Zinc is definitely being OXIDIZED (losing electrons) in this reaction -- its role as 'reducing agent' refers to what it does to the other substance, not what happens to itself.

options.text: The terms 'oxidizing agent' and 'reducing agent' are actually interchangeable and mean the same thing
options.feedback: These terms are NOT interchangeable -- a reducing agent gets oxidized while causing reduction in another substance, and an oxidizing agent gets reduced while causing oxidation in another substance.

hints.hard: Naming conventions for these agent terms describe the EFFECT a substance has on its reaction partner, not the change happening to the substance itself.
hints.medium: Zinc's own electron loss is exactly what allows copper to gain electrons and become reduced -- so zinc 'causes' the reduction.
hints.easy: Zinc losing its own electrons is exactly what lets copper gain electrons and get reduced.

questions.text: The ideal gas law is written as PV = nRT. What does the 'V' represent?

options.text: Volume of the gas
options.feedback: Correct -- V represents the volume occupied by the gas.

options.text: Velocity of the gas particles
options.feedback: Velocity isn't a direct variable in this equation -- V specifically stands for volume here.

options.text: The number of moles of gas
options.feedback: That's represented by 'n' in the equation, not 'V'.

options.text: The temperature of the gas
options.feedback: That's represented by 'T' in the equation, not 'V'.

questions.text: According to the ideal gas law (PV = nRT), if the number of moles (n) and temperature (T) stay constant, what happens to pressure (P) if volume (V) decreases?

options.text: Pressure increases
options.feedback: Correct -- since PV must equal the constant nRT, decreasing V requires P to increase proportionally to maintain that balance (this is also known as Boyle's Law).

options.text: Pressure decreases
options.feedback: This is backwards -- with nRT held constant, DECREASING volume actually requires pressure to INCREASE, not decrease, to keep PV constant.

options.text: Pressure stays exactly the same
options.feedback: Since PV must remain equal to the constant nRT, changing V without changing P would break that equality -- pressure must adjust.

options.text: Pressure becomes zero
options.feedback: Pressure doesn't drop to zero -- it increases as volume decreases, following the inverse relationship described by the ideal gas law.

hints.hard: Since the product of pressure and volume must remain proportional to the constant nRT term, consider how a decrease in one factor must be compensated by the other.
hints.medium: Since n and T aren't changing, P times V has to stay the same -- so if V goes down, P must go up.
hints.easy: If V goes down and the other side of the equation stays the same, P must go up to balance it.

questions.text: A sealed rigid container holds gas at a fixed volume. If you heat the gas, increasing its temperature, what happens to the pressure inside the container, and why might this be dangerous?

options.text: Pressure increases proportionally with temperature (since volume can't change in a rigid container), and if pressure rises too high, it could exceed the container's structural strength and cause it to rupture
options.feedback: Correct -- since V and n are fixed, PV=nRT shows P must rise directly with T, which is exactly why sealed containers exposed to heat (like aerosol cans in fire) pose a real explosion risk.

options.text: Pressure stays exactly the same regardless of temperature, since the container is rigid
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- with volume fixed, increasing temperature necessarily increases pressure, according to the ideal gas law relationship.

options.text: Pressure decreases as temperature increases in a sealed rigid container
options.feedback: This is backwards -- with volume held constant, increasing temperature causes pressure to INCREASE, not decrease.

options.text: There is no real danger, since gas pressure cannot damage a rigid container
options.feedback: This is actually a real and significant danger -- sealed containers can rupture or explode if internal pressure builds up too high due to heating, which is why aerosol cans warn against exposure to heat.

hints.hard: With volume and moles fixed, isolate the direct proportional relationship between pressure and temperature implied by the ideal gas law equation.
hints.medium: Since the container's volume can't change, and n stays the same, increasing T directly forces P to increase too.
hints.easy: Since the container's volume can't change, heating the gas directly increases the pressure inside.

questions.text: What does it mean for a solution to be 'saturated'?

options.text: It contains the maximum amount of dissolved solute possible at that temperature

options.text: It contains no dissolved solute at all

options.text: It has reached its boiling point

options.text: It has been heated to a very high temperature
options.feedback: Temperature affects solubility, but 'saturated' specifically refers to reaching a maximum dissolved solute amount, not a specific temperature.

questions.text: For most solid solutes dissolving in water, increasing the temperature typically increases solubility. If you have a saturated sugar-water solution at room temperature and then heat it, what will likely happen?

options.text: The solution can now dissolve additional sugar, since higher temperature typically increases a solid solute's solubility
options.feedback: Correct -- since heating generally increases solubility for solid solutes like sugar, the solution becomes capable of dissolving more solute than it could at the lower temperature.

options.text: The dissolved sugar will immediately come out of solution and form solid crystals
options.feedback: This is backwards -- for most solids, HEATING increases solubility (allowing MORE to dissolve), rather than causing dissolved solute to crystallize out.

options.text: Temperature changes have no effect on how much sugar can dissolve
options.feedback: Temperature very much affects solubility for most solutes -- for solids like sugar, increasing temperature typically increases how much can dissolve.

options.text: The solution will instantly boil away completely, leaving only solid sugar

hints.hard: Consider the general relationship between temperature and solubility for most solid solutes dissolving in a liquid solvent.
hints.medium: For most solids dissolving in water, hotter water can generally hold more dissolved solute than cooler water.
hints.easy: Hotter water can generally dissolve more sugar than cooler water can.

questions.text: If you make a saturated sugar solution at a high temperature and then let it cool slowly and undisturbed, sometimes MORE sugar remains dissolved than the solution's normal saturation point at that lower temperature would allow. What is this unstable condition called, and why can it occur?

options.text: A supersaturated solution -- it occurs when the solution cools without a nucleation site (like a sugar crystal or disturbance) to trigger the excess solute crystallizing back out
options.feedback: Correct -- without a trigger point for crystal formation, excess dissolved solute can remain suspended in solution beyond its normal solubility limit, creating an unstable, supersaturated state (used in rock candy making).

options.text: This condition is impossible and could never actually occur in a real solution
options.feedback: This is a real, well-documented phenomenon called supersaturation, commonly demonstrated with sugar or salt solutions (and used to make rock candy).

options.text: This is simply an ordinary unsaturated solution, nothing unusual is happening
options.feedback: This is actually an unusual, UNSTABLE state (supersaturation) exceeding the normal saturation limit at that temperature, not a typical unsaturated solution.

options.text: This occurs because the sugar chemically transforms into a completely different, more soluble substance
options.feedback: No chemical transformation of the sugar occurs -- the excess dissolved sugar is simply in an unstable physical state, lacking a trigger point for crystallization.

hints.hard: Consider what physical trigger point is typically required to initiate crystallization, and what happens to dissolved solute when that trigger is absent during cooling.
hints.medium: Without something like a tiny crystal or a disturbance to 'kick off' the process, the extra dissolved sugar can stay dissolved even past its normal limit.
hints.easy: Without something to 'kick off' crystal formation, extra dissolved sugar can stay dissolved past its normal limit.

questions.text: What are isotopes?

questions.text: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both isotopes of carbon. Given that carbon always has 6 protons, how do these two isotopes differ?

options.text: Carbon-14 has 2 fewer electrons than Carbon-12

options.text: There is actually no real difference between Carbon-12 and Carbon-14
